case_study_insert.main_stem: Bayharbour Hotels (BHR) is a partnership in the hospitality sector, running a waterside hotel and rooftop restaurant and employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2010 by Tomas Lindqvist, BHR uses a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership, so the senior partners set service standards for reception and kitchen teams. BHR plans to invest $880,000 in a 45-room extension with a rooftop restaurant, financed by a $580,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $200,000 a year, a variable cost of $28 a unit and a selling price of $92, and currently produces 13,000 units a year, each a booked room-night. BHR faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 10% and food waste in the restaurant is rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Waste Report — Q4 2025: BHR served 3,250 room-nights last quarter at 74% occupancy, down from 81% a year earlier. Kitchen food waste rose to 88 kg per week from 54 kg. Complaints about breakfast quality rose to 27 per month from 16. Guest rating fell from 4.5 to 4.1 out of 5. A survey of 550 guests found that 64% would pay up to $7 more for locally sourced breakfasts and 53% value active waste reduction. Records show 12 of 36 staff have not completed on-the-job training in food hygiene; off-the-job training courses cost $280 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Bayharbour Hotels as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Hospitality Bulletin (July 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing interest on BHR's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $12.60 to $13.42 per hour, raising wages for BHR's 36 staff. (3) Food and beverage input costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, while domestic hotel demand grew 3.1% and business travel spending rose 2.4%.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for BHR of using $300,000 retained profit alongside the $580,000 bank loan to fund the extension.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Putting $300,000 retained profit into the $880,000 extension reduces the sum BHR must borrow, so interest and repayments on the $580,000 loan are lower and more of the $64 contribution from each room-night stays in the partnership. With fixed costs of $200,000 a year already to meet, a smaller debt service protects the cash needed to run the rooftop restaurant while the 45 new rooms are filling.

Point 2: Retained profit is immediately available and carries no lender conditions, letting Tomas Lindqvist and the partners proceed without a further credit application or collateral. It also keeps decision-making inside the partnership. Holding $300,000 back from external finance leaves BHR better placed to absorb the 10% absenteeism and the $280 per employee hygiene-training costs, so the existing hotel is not starved of funds while the extension is built. As a partnership, BHR also avoids the market scrutiny that a public listing would bring.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of using retained profit alongside debt identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to BHR's $880,000 extension, room-night economics and staffing.

questions.question_text: BHR is promoting its new rooftop restaurant and 45-room extension. Consider a national radio campaign, local newspaper sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should BHR choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National radio campaign: Radio can build quick awareness of the rooftop restaurant across a wide audience and is relatively cheap. Most listeners, however, are outside travelling distance of BHR's waterside hotel, so the spend is poorly targeted for a partnership with a $580,000 loan. With occupancy down from 81% to 74%, BHR needs bookings from people who can actually stay, not mass hearership.

Local newspaper sponsorship: Sponsoring local papers or events reaches nearby guests cheaply and suits a hotel with a strong regional trade. Its reach is narrow, however, and the 64% of 550 surveyed guests willing to pay $7 more for local breakfasts are not only local residents; print also lacks the visual impact needed to sell a rooftop view.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and travel influencers can show the restaurant and locally sourced breakfasts to the 53% of surveyed guests who value waste reduction, with trackable engagement at low cost. Results build gradually and depend on credible influencers, but the message can be targeted at travellers planning a stay.

Recommendation: BHR should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the survey-identified segment, supports the $7 premium and can be measured, unlike radio. Radio is rejected as untargeted and newspaper sponsorship as too narrow to lift occupancy from 74% and justify the $880,000 extension. Influencer content can be reused on BHR's booking page and measured against the 27 breakfast complaints and the 4.1 rating, which radio and press cannot track for a partnership with a $580,000 loan and 74% occupancy.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal reference to BHR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two options with some application to BHR's launch and occupancy.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why radio and newspapers are rejected.

questions.question_text: BHR's absenteeism has reached 10% and kitchen food waste is rising. Explain two benefits for BHR of using autocratic leadership to tackle these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets the senior partners set clear portion sizes and waste-monitoring rules immediately, which can cut the 88 kg of weekly food waste without waiting for team consensus. In a hierarchical structure, firm instructions reach the kitchen quickly, helping protect the $64 contribution on each room-night and the $92 room price while the rooftop restaurant opens.

Point 2: When absenteeism reaches 10%, quick decisions about covering shifts and reallocating reception duties keep the hotel running smoothly, reducing disruption to the 3,250 room-nights served last quarter. Clear standards also give staff certainty about expectations, which can reduce the 27 breakfast complaints and support the 4.1 guest rating while the $580,000 loan is serviced. The partners can set a clear waste-reduction target that all 36 staff follow, making the 88 kg a visible measure of progress. Decisive action is appropriate while the rating is under pressure during an $880,000 expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of autocratic leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to BHR's absence, waste and service standards.

questions.question_text: BHR must train 12 kitchen staff in food-hygiene procedures for the new restaurant. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should BHR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training in BHR's own kitchen is directly relevant to its hygiene standards, costs no fees and keeps all 12 staff preparing meals while they learn, which protects service during the 3,250 room-nights handled last quarter. It can cut the 27 breakfast complaints quickly. Drawbacks are that trainers are also working, so the kitchen may slow, and bad habits can spread unless partners inspect; formal certification may be weak if guests ask for proof.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $280 per employee gives structured, up-to-date hygiene skills and a recognised certificate for 12 staff, costing $3,360 — small against the $880,000 extension. It removes staff from the kitchen while occupancy is 74%, threatening service, and generic content may not match BHR's menu, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: BHR should choose on-the-job training with short college certification later. It is cheaper, kitchen-specific and avoids losing 12 of 36 staff while absence is 10%; full off-the-job training is rejected because the disruption and $3,360 fee are less justified than practical training where the food is actually prepared. The senior partners should inspect portions and hygiene routines daily during the rollout so the 27 complaints do not rise, and any trainee below standard should be paired with an experienced chef. If guests ask for evidence, short college certification for the 12 staff can be bought later for $3,360 from retained profit, leaving the $580,000 loan untouched and the kitchen running at 74% occupancy while 13,000 room-nights are sold.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to BHR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of BHR's hygiene and waste issues.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to BHR's kitchen.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BHR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $200,000 ÷ ($92 − $28) = $200,000 ÷ $64 = 3,125 units. Answer: break-even output is 3,125 room-nights a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $92 − $28 = $64. Answer: contribution per unit is $64.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BHR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare 3,125-unit break-even with actual output of 13,000 room-nights: the margin of safety is 9,875 room-nights, showing the 45-room extension can be added without immediate loss risk.
2. Use the $64 contribution to test pricing: the $7 locally sourced breakfast premium would lift contribution to $71, which can be checked against the 64% of 550 surveyed guests who support it.
3. Check loan capacity: with 3,125 room-nights needed to break even, the $580,000 repayment is coverable, so partners can set monthly occupancy targets to protect the cushion.
4. Benchmark unit cost: $200,000 ÷ 13,000 units + $28 = $43.38 a room-night, a figure to track for the effect of the 8.9% food-cost inflation and the 88 kg weekly waste before they erode the $64 contribution.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 3,125 room-nights | (ii) Contribution per unit = $64 | (iii) Four uses: 9,875-room-night margin of safety, $7 breakfast-premium modelling, $580,000 loan feasibility and $43.38 unit-cost benchmarking.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BHR's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has BHR's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.32 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.82 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.08 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $48,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $22,000 cash = $130,000. 2025 current assets = $30,000 + $95,000 + $40,000 = $165,000. 2024: $130,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.30; 2025: $165,000 ÷ $125,000 = 1.32. Excluding inventories: 2024 ($130,000 − $48,000) ÷ $100,000 = $82,000 ÷ $100,000 = 0.82; 2025 ($165,000 − $30,000) ÷ $125,000 = $135,000 ÷ $125,000 = 1.08.

Evaluation: Liquidity improved, though the first measure moved only slightly from 1.30 to 1.32 because current liabilities rose from $100,000 to $125,000 alongside assets. The second measure rose more meaningfully from 0.82 to 1.08, meaning BHR now covers short-term debts without relying on selling the restaurant's inventories — important when $880,000 is being spent on the extension. Cash doubled from $22,000 to $40,000, giving a buffer for the $580,000 loan. Receivables did rise from $60,000 to $95,000, however, so some of the gain depends on collecting from customers; credit control should be watched.

Conclusion: BHR's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the acid test now exceeds 1, showing stronger short-term solvency. The main caution is rising receivables, which should be managed as the new rooms absorb cash. The $300,000 retained profit in the extension should be rebuilt before further borrowing, because $40,000 of cash is a thin buffer against a $580,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of inventories, cash, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BHR of introducing locally sourced breakfasts priced up to $7 higher.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 550 guests found that 64% would pay up to $7 more for locally sourced breakfasts and 53% value waste reduction. The premium can lift contribution from $64 towards $71 a room-night, helping cover $200,000 fixed costs and the $580,000 loan, while strengthening the rooftop restaurant's appeal and the 74% occupancy rate.

Disadvantage: Local ingredients often cost more and supply is less reliable, which could raise the $28 variable cost and offset the $7 premium. If the kitchen cannot deliver consistent quality, the 27 breakfast complaints and 4.1 guest rating could worsen, and the 88 kg weekly food waste might not fall, undermining the $880,000 restaurant investment. Locally sourced menus also support the partnership's brand and the 53% who value waste reduction, helping restore the 4.1 rating. If the $7 premium holds, contribution rises from $64 toward $71 and the kitchen can target lower waste and protect the 4.1 rating.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using BHR's survey, costs and waste data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 8.9% rise in food and beverage costs will affect BHR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If BHR's $580,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.75% of $580,000 = $4,350 a year (0.0075 × $580,000). That is modest next to fixed costs of $200,000 a year and would be zero if the loan were fixed. Higher rates may also reduce business travel spending, but the direct cost can be limited by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $13.42 per hour): With a workforce of 36, the rise increases the wage bill for kitchen and reception staff and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an honest annual total cannot be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity of 13,000 room-nights ÷ 36 staff = 361.11 room-nights per worker. If that holds, the cost is spread over output; with 10% absence it could raise unit labour cost and shrink the $64 contribution.

Food and beverage inflation (8.9%): The $28 variable cost per room-night is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is defensible: if the whole $28 rose 8.9%, that is 0.089 × $28 = $2.49 a room-night, and at 13,000 room-nights about $32,370 a year. It touches every booking and directly threatens the contribution that funds the $880,000 extension; the $7 breakfast premium recovers only part of it.

Conclusion: The 8.9% rise in food and beverage costs will have the greatest impact because it compounds over all 13,000 room-nights and erodes the $64 contribution, while the interest rise is a bounded $4,350 and the wage rise can be offset if 361.11 room-nights per worker is maintained.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to BHR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on BHR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in BHR's context with a justified greatest-impact judgment and reasons why the others are smaller.
